UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
V. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION
FOR LEAVE TO FILE SUR-REPLY

I. INTRODUCTION

Plaintiff does not seek another round of argument on Meta’s Motion to Dismiss. Meta’s
Reply (ECF No. 39) largely reiterates or develops arguments advanced in its opening
memorandum (ECF No. 22), or responds to arguments in Plaintiff’s opposition (ECF No. 30).
Plaintiff seeks no additional briefing on those matters.

One argument is different. Meta argues for the first time in reply that Count IV fails because
Plaintiff “has not identified any non-speculative opportunity for him to provide testimony in any
action” and because the FAC supposedly fails to identify “any actual testimony in federal court
that Plaintiff has or likely will offer.” ECF No. 39 at 7. Meta’s opening memorandum did not
advance that proposed pleading requirement. Plaintiff therefore has had no opportunity to address

it. The Proposed Sur-Reply is confined to that issue.

The Proposed Sur-Reply requires no new evidence. The new argument is answered by the

First Amended Complaint itself.

Il. STANDARD

Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) permits an opening memorandum, an opposition, and a reply.
Beyond those three, “[nJo further briefs or written communications may be filed without first
obtaining leave of Court.” E.D. Va. Loc. Civ. R. 7(F)(1).

This Court has stated the governing principles. “[A]llowing a surreply is within the court’s
discretion.” Taylor v. Revature LLC, No. 1:22-cv-1153 (RDA/WBP), Dkt. 81, at 8-9 (E.D. Va.
Mar. 5, 2025) (quoting Adams v. Applied Bus. Servs., 2019 WL 7817080, at *1 (E.D. Va. Aug. 30,
2019)). In deciding whether to exercise that discretion, the Court “consider[s] whether prejudice
will result from the court considering a new argument without the opposing party’s having an
opportunity to respond.” Id. at 9. “To cure any such prejudice, a surreply is appropriate where ‘a
party brings forth new material or deploys new arguments in a reply brief.’” Id. (quoting Clawson
v. FedEx Ground Package Sys., Inc., 451 F. Supp. 2d 731, 734 (D. Md. 2006)). A sur-reply is not
appropriate where the reply merely “further support[s] an argument made in [the] opening brief”
or responds to arguments first raised in the opposition. Id. Sur-replies “are generally disfavored”
and are reserved for “rare instances.” Id. (quoting Steele v. Johns Hopkins Health Sys. Corp., 2020
WL 4471710, at *2 (D. Md. Aug. 4, 2020)).

The Court applied those principles this year in SkyBell Technologies, Inc. v. Alarm.com,
Inc., No. 1:25-cv-01105 (RDA/WBP), Dkt. 32 (E.D. Va. Mar. 4, 2026). There, whether the reply
raised new arguments was “a closer call.” Id. at 8. The Court granted leave anyway, reasoning that
considering the sur-reply would “accomplish dispositional efficiency and . . . avoid prejudice to
either party.” Id. Plaintiff’s application identifies the new proposition, the page on which it first

appears, and the confined response he seeks to make.

Ill, META FIRST ADVANCED THE PROSPECTIVE-TESTIMONY REQUIREMENT
IN REPLY

The briefing progressed in three steps.

First, Meta’s opening memorandum attacked injury. It argued that Plaintiff had not pleaded
facts showing that the letters actually impaired his ability to testify or pursue his claims, because
he continued to litigate both actions. ECF No. 22 at 12. In a footnote, Meta suggested that
“attending court” might require physical presence at a proceeding. Id. at 12 n.1. Meta did not argue
that a prospective witness must plead a presently identifiable, sufficiently certain, “non-
speculative” future occasion to testify. It did not argue that Count IV fails for want of allegations
identifying testimony Plaintiff “has or likely will offer.” It did not use the later dismissal of one
underlying action, or the pendency of a motion to dismiss in the other, as a test of Plaintiff’s
witness status when the alleged conduct occurred.

Second, Plaintiff’s opposition answered the injury argument by pointing to the FAC’s
allegations of functional impairment despite continued prosecution. ECF No. 30 at 18—19. Plaintiff
also explained that the conditional physical-presence footnote did not reach the statute’s separate
protection against deterring testimony, because the FAC pleads Plaintiff’s prospective-witness
status and a purpose to deter that testimony. Id. at 20—21.

Third, Meta’s Reply introduced a new proposition. Meta now contends that “Plaintiff has
not identified any non-speculative opportunity for him to provide testimony in any action,” and
that “[t]he FAC’s failure to identify any actual testimony in federal court that Plaintiff has or likely
will offer independently dooms Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim.” ECF No. 39 at 7. Meta supports
that proposition with procedural developments occurring after the alleged April 22, 2026 conduct:
the dismissal of the 286 Action and the pending motion to dismiss in the 376 Action, from which

Meta concludes that “it is likely that no such potential testimony will ever come to fruition.” Id.

The distinction is narrow but consequential. An argument that Plaintiff failed to plead
injury from alleged intimidation is different from an argument that Plaintiff was insufficiently a
prospective witness because future testimony was not certain enough to occur. The opening
argument concerned whether the alleged intimidation caused the required injury. The Reply adds
a different proposition: that the prospective-testimony theory independently fails because the FAC
identifies no sufficiently certain future testimony. Meta itself calls that proposition independently
dispositive. ECF No. 39 at 7.

Plaintiff acknowledges that Meta’s page-7 discussion begins by responding to the
opposition’s reliance on the testimony branch. But the subject was already joined; the new
independent ground for dismissal was not. The FAC pleaded Plaintiff’s prospective-witness status
from the outset. ECF No. 5 4 31, 158-160. Meta had that pleading when it filed its opening
memorandum and chose to attack injury. The opposition did not introduce a new theory; it
identified an existing allegation. What is new is Meta’s contention that Count IV independently
fails unless the FAC identifies testimony sufficiently certain or likely to occur. Plaintiff has had

no prior opportunity to address that contention.

IV. ‘THE PROPOSED SUR-REPLY IS CONFINED TO THE NEW ISSUE

Exhibit A answers the new proposition from the four comers of the FAC. It quotes the
paragraphs that plead Plaintiff’s prospective-witness status, the subjects of his expected swom
testimony, Defendants’ knowledge of that status, and the alleged purpose of deterring that
testimony. ECF No. 5 § 27, 31, 51-54, 158-160. It applies the Rule 12(b)(6) standard to those
allegations. It does not revisit Meta’s previously briefed arguments concerning agreement,
intimidation, or Plaintiffs continued litigation as evidence of injury. It attaches no declaration,
introduces no new evidence, and relies only on the existing Rule 12 record, principally the FAC

and Meta’s Reply.

Meta’s argument does not identify an omitted allegation. It asks the Court to disregard an
allegation that is already there. A short response confined to that point does not delay the Motion
to Dismiss. It permits the Court to decide the newly raised issue on a complete adversarial
presentation, which is the purpose the Court identified in SkyBell.

V. CONCLUSION
The Court should grant leave under Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) to file the Proposed Sur-Reply

attached to the Motion as Exhibit A, and should deem it filed as of the date of the Court’s Order.
